clue.text: Outsize monocular troglodyte

parts.note: a giant with a single eye who lives in a cave: the Cyclops whom Odysseus blinds in the Odyssey

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a plain description dressed in grand Latinate words: 'outsize' for giant, 'monocular' for one-eyed, 'troglodyte' for cave-dweller.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's Cyclops is a one-eyed giant who keeps Odysseus and his men penned in his cave.

clue.text: Poet inclined to pontificate?

definitions.meaning: Alexander, the eighteenth-century English poet of The Rape of the Lock
the head of the Roman Catholic Church is the pontiff, who by office pontificates

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the joke: to pontificate is to hold forth pompously, but literally it is what a pontiff does.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander of that surname was a poet, and the Holy Father is the one figure whose job is literally to pontificate.

clue.text: "The rain is on our —, / We do not run for prize" (Sorley)

definitions.text: "The rain is on our —, / We do not run for prize" (Sorley)

parts.words: "The rain is on our —, / We do not run for prize" (Sorley)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Charles Sorley's poem The Song of the Ungirt Runners: the missing word is the body part the rain falls on as the runners go

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: supply the missing word from the poem by Charles Sorley, a poet killed in the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: The line in Sorley's poem reads that the rain falls on the runners' mouths, completing the quotation.

clue.text: What Eliot thought the "dialect of the tribe" achieved under the impulsion of speech

definitions.text: What Eliot thought the "dialect of the tribe" achieved under the impulsion of speech

parts.words: What Eliot thought the "dialect of the tribe" achieved under the impulsion of speech
parts.note: refers to Little Gidding, where Eliot writes that speech impelled us to purify the dialect of the tribe; the clue asks for the noun form of that verb

explanation.walkthrough: From Four Quartets: 'Since our concern was speech, and speech impelled us / To purify the dialect of the tribe'. Turn the verb into its noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's line says speech drove poets to cleanse the tribe's dialect, so what the dialect underwent was a cleansing.

clue.text: Upset a seer, and wipe it out

indicators.note: something upset is overturned and thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shocks a prophet and then tries to blot out what they did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges the letters of A SEER.
explanation.definitionFit: To delete something is to wipe it out, removing all trace.

clue.text: Most like Brutus' cut

parts.note: recalls Mark Antony's speech in Julius Caesar, calling Brutus's stab the most cruel cut of all, with Shakespeare's double superlative

explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar Antony's double superlative 'most unkindest' is the famous phrase; 'Most like' tells you to find the superlative used of Brutus's cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony calls Brutus's wound 'the most unkindest cut of all', so the word that sits after 'most' in that line is wanted.

clue.text: Frank is writer on nothing

indicators.note: in an across clue the writer placed on nothing comes after it

parts.note: nothing is zero, written as the letter O
a pen is the instrument one writes with

explanation.surface: A candid statement that some author is utterly worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' here means placed after: PEN follows O.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frank means being candid and forthright, holding nothing back.

clue.text: Past holds strangely simple example of something overwritten- (5)

indicators.note: the word past holds the other letters within it, acting as a container
simple behaving strangely means its letters are rearranged into an odd order

explanation.surface: History contains a plain specimen of something that has been written over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Past' looks like the time word but is just the container; 'strangely' scrambles the letters of 'simple', and 'holds' wraps the first word round the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A manuscript whose original text was scraped off and written over is the classic instance of overwriting.

clue.text: Unintelligible stuff in Japanese drama? (actually, it's straightforward)

parts.note: Noh, also spelt No, is the classical masked drama of Japan
meaningless talk is nonsense

explanation.surface: A puzzled theatregoer at a Noh play finds it baffling, then admits it is really quite simple.
explanation.walkthrough: NO is the usual crossword spelling of Noh, the classical Japanese masked drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with none of that rubbish about it is direct and businesslike, plain and simple.

clue.text: Journal supports less expensive books ".

parts.note: a newspaper or journal is a paper
to support someone is to back them

explanation.surface: A newspaper endorses cheaper editions of books.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft-covered editions cost less than hardbacks.

clue.text: Lords fall, men destroyed, for Defoe protagonist

indicators.note: destroyed means the words are broken up and their letters rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: Aristocrats collapse and their men are ruined, all for the sake of a novel's heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroyed' rearranges the letters of LORDS, FALL and MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Defoe's 1722 novel follows its title heroine through a life of crime and marriages.

clue.text: PM and followers immortalized by Powell

parts.note: p.m. stands for post meridiem, the hours after midday
a leader's followers are their men

explanation.surface: A prime minister and his entourage are made famous by a politician named Powell.
explanation.walkthrough: PM looks like Prime Minister and Powell like the politician Enoch Powell; in fact PM is the time of day and Powell is the novelist Anthony Powell, whose first novel this is.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Powell's first novel (1931) is a satire on idle young Londoners, so its title is fixed in print by him.

clue.text: Rectories I turn inside out for desk

indicators.note: turning the rectories inside out means totally rearranging what makes them up

explanation.surface: Someone ransacks vicarages hunting for a writing desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn inside out' rearranges the letters of RECTORIES and I.
explanation.definitionFit: A writing bureau with drawers and a flap is a kind of desk.

clue.text: "A fate worse than marriage. A sort of eternal " (Alan Ayckbourn)

definitions.text: "A fate worse than marriage. A sort of eternal " (Alan Ayckbourn)

parts.words: "A fate worse than marriage. A sort of eternal " (Alan Ayckbourn)
parts.note: a gap-fill from the playwright Alan Ayckbourn: the missing word is the state of being promised but not yet wed

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: supply the word missing at the end of Ayckbourn's line, the period between a proposal and the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayckbourn's joke is that a betrothal that never ends is worse than marrying.

clue.text: Related poems for voices (but the best-known one was made for two?)

definitions.meaning: a set of linked poems set to music for a singer

definitions.text: the best-known one was made for two?
definitions.meaning: the popular song Daisy Bell sings of a bicycle built for two, the most famous bike in any song

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the phrase literally: a bicycle that appears in a song, and the famous one is the tandem of Daisy Bell ('a bicycle made for two').
explanation.definitionFit: A linked set of art songs is so named, and the bicycle made for two in Daisy Bell is literally a bike in a song.

clue.text: Margaret of Newcastle, whom Pepys thought "mad, conceited and ridiculous"

definitions.text: Margaret of Newcastle, whom Pepys thought "mad, conceited and ridiculous"

parts.words: Margaret of Newcastle, whom Pepys thought "mad, conceited and ridiculous"
parts.note: the seventeenth-century Duchess of Newcastle, a writer and philosopher whom the diarist Samuel Pepys mocked; the clue wants her family surname

explanation.walkthrough: A general-knowledge clue: the Duchess's married surname is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Lucas married William, Duke of Newcastle, and wrote under her married surname.

clue.text: Anthem composer uses strong thread

definitions.meaning: Claude Joseph Rouget de ... wrote the Marseillaise, the French national anthem
a fine, tough twisted cotton thread used for stockings

explanation.definitionFit: Rouget de Lisle composed France's national anthem, and the same word names a hard-twisted cotton yarn.

clue.text: Respond — and put on play again?

definitions.meaning: to respond is to give a reply or reaction
to act a play once more

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the split reading: RE (again) plus ACT (put on a play).
explanation.definitionFit: Responding is replying to a stimulus, and split as re-act the word means performing again.

clue.text: Last visit, perhaps, of believers in life force

indicators.note: perhaps signals that these letters might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A final call paid, perhaps, to some mystics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges the letters of LAST VISIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitalism is the doctrine that living things have a vital principle beyond chemistry.

clue.text: The satellite's shade, recorded by Collins (9)

parts.note: taken as written
the Moon is the Earth's satellite, with the possessive S kept
a shade of a colour is a tone

explanation.surface: The colour of the Moon is noted down by someone named Collins.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's of 'satellite's' supplies a letter here. Collins is Wilkie Collins, whose 1868 novel is often called the first English detective novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilkie Collins wrote the 1868 novel about a stolen Indian diamond.

clue.text: Instruct a pirate ()

definitions.meaning: to instruct is to give lessons
Edward ..., better known as Blackbeard, the early eighteenth-century pirate

explanation.definitionFit: To instruct is to give lessons, and Edward Teach was the real name of the pirate Blackbeard.

clue.text: Watercolour ()

parts.note: one word read as two: the Latin for water, and also a pale blue-green colour

explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for water is also the name of a blue-green tint, so the word is both water and colour.

clue.text: Barbara Pym's suitably venerable spinster sisters

definitions.text: Barbara Pym's suitably venerable spinster sisters

parts.words: Barbara Pym's suitably venerable spinster sisters
parts.note: Belinda and Harriet, the unmarried sisters of Pym's Some Tame Gazelle, share their surname with the Venerable monk-historian of Jarrow

explanation.walkthrough: 'Suitably venerable' points to the Venerable Bede, the eighth-century monk and historian of England, whose name Pym gave her sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: The sisters' surname is that of the Anglo-Saxon historian always styled 'the Venerable', hence 'suitably venerable'.

clue.text: Eastertide newcomers, including Richard Jefferies's farmer

indicators.note: the words Eastertide newcomers include the wanted letters inside them, across the word break

explanation.surface: New arrivals at Easter are joined by a farmer from a Jefferies novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Including' marks letters running across EastertIDE Newcomers.
explanation.definitionFit: The farmer in Richard Jefferies's novel Amaryllis at the Fair bears this surname.

clue.text: Worries concealed by resentment in rogue's sort of adventures

definitions.note: the definition is the kind of story told, read as describing such adventures

indicators.note: worries hidden by resentment sit inside it, enclosed within it

parts.note: pique is a feeling of irritation or resentment
worries are cares

explanation.surface: Anxieties buried under bitterness find an outlet in a scoundrel's escapades.
explanation.walkthrough: The picaro is the Spanish rogue-hero; 'concealed by' has the resentment word wrap round the worries word.
explanation.definitionFit: The picaresque genre, from Spanish picaro (rogue), recounts the episodic adventures of a likeable rascal.

clue.text: "… to enhance the environment in which he ——, sleeps, and watches television" (Germaine Greer)

definitions.text: "… to enhance the environment in which he ——, sleeps, and watches television" (Germaine Greer)

parts.words: "… to enhance the environment in which he ——, sleeps, and watches television" (Germaine Greer)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Germaine Greer: the missing word is the daily activity listed beside sleeping and watching TV, taking meals

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: supply the verb Greer pairs with sleeping and watching television in describing a husband's home life.
explanation.definitionFit: Alongside sleeping and watching television, the missing verb is taking food, consuming meals.

clue.text: Brendan Behan's a long time following the army

definitions.note: possessive: the play that is Brendan Behan's

indicators.note: the long time follows the army in the answer, coming after it

parts.note: taken as written
host is an old word for an army, as in the heavenly host
an age is a very long time

explanation.surface: Ages after the troops have marched off, someone named Behan is still waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: Host is an old word for an army. Brendan Behan's 1958 play was first staged in Irish as An Giall.
explanation.definitionFit: Brendan Behan, the Irish playwright, wrote this 1958 play about a captive British soldier in Dublin.
